title: Responses protocol differentials and runtime fallbacks: field-level mapping & stream semantics
creator: Maya Chen
description: Objective: Produce a detailed compatibility mapping between Redwood's Responses-compatible surface and the OpenAI Responses API. Focus on three hard areas: streaming event semantics (chunk framing, finalization markers, partial deltas), function/tool call lifecycle (open/continue/complete events + ambiguous arg typing), and structured-output schemas (JSON validation vs freeform 'content' fields). Deliverables: mapping doc, shim design for Node + Rust SDKs, automated conformance tests, and a canary rollout plan that exercises runtime fallbacks when parity gaps are hit.
acceptance_criteria: Field-level mapping doc that lists every top-level and nested field difference and proposed normalized shape
Streaming behavior spec with test vectors for early termination, interim deltas, and event ordering
Function-call lifecycle state machine and event mapping (open/emit/complete/error) documented
Prototype shim implemented for Node SDK with togglable translation mode and unit tests
Conformance test suite that runs against both OpenAI Responses (mock) and Redwood runtime and flags mismatches
Canary rollout plan including per-tenant metric thresholds and automatic fallback rules
decisions: Normalize on a compact intermediate model for translation: {event_type, payload, meta} instead of trying one-to-one mapping to OpenAI field names
Implement finalization token: an explicit 'response_complete' event emitted by runtime when KV cache flush and model EOS observed
Treat function/tool 'args' as opaque string in shim, but include inferred 'arg_schema' metadata when model emits structured tokens to aid downstream validators
Fallback policy: route to legacy 'responses-v0-compat' model variant when structural validation fails and retry with lossy mapping disabled
design_tradeoffs: One-to-one mapping keeps fidelity but multiplies edge cases across multiple model families; intermediate model simplifies shims but loses some vendor-specific hints
Synchronous validation on the runtime path would block low-latency streams; we prefer async validation with fast heuristics in the hot path and full validation during post-processing
Conservative function-call mapping reduces accidental tool abuse but requires richer telemetry to reconstruct intent for debugging
implementation_notes: Stream framing: adopt 4 event classes: 'delta', 'tool_event', 'meta', 'response_complete'. Each framed as newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) in the streaming protocol to match current Redwood streaming transport
Backpressure: ensure SDKs expose a 'pause' callback that's triggered when downstream validators apply synchronous checks
KV cache semantics: do not attempt to persist partial tool outputs; only persist after a response_complete event and KV flush marker
Error mapping: map OpenAI 'invalid_request_error' -> 'client_schema_error', 'rate_limit' -> 'quota_exceeded' with preserved original code and hint in meta
test_plan: Create a mock OpenAI Responses server with 40+ behavior vectors (stream order inversion, mid-stream function open/close, truncated JSON payloads)
Add automated tests to CI that run the mock against the shim and Redwood runtime; expected outcomes captured in golden files
Performance tests to ensure shim adds <2ms median overhead per token for typical chat streams
Chaos test: inject delayed response_complete events to verify fallback triggers and no silent hangs
canary_plan: Canary cohort: 2% of new hosted API tenants + internal dev tenants
Metrics to watch: structured_output_validation_fail_rate, fallback_rate, stream_error_rate, p95_stream_latency
Kill criteria: fallback_rate > 1% for 30m, or structured_output_validation_fail_rate increase > 0.5% relative to baseline
Rollback: instant traffic re-route to responses-legacy endpoint and open pager if criteria met
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Uncaught streaming ordering differences cause downstream tool mis-invocations. Mitigation: add sequence numbers in shim meta and runtime instrumentation to reconcile ordering.
Risk: Schema-heavy workloads induce higher CPU for validation. Mitigation: provide optional 'validation_level' per-tenant (none, fast, strict) and fall back to async validation for 'fast'
Risk: Customers relying on exact OpenAI error text might see different wording. Mitigation: preserve original error.message in 'meta.original_error' field for auditability
